While some evidence already points to biological differences in how men's and women’s immune systems respond, the doctor noted that the issue "deserves a little bit more attention" from researchers. "At the end of the day, there is no evidence ... that men have more severe symptoms, suffer more, or experience more pain or discomfort when it comes to the flu, colds or other respiratory viruses and viral illnesses ," she said. "It is clear that Miss Becker had ended the hopes of a relationship and was afraid of Kanmacher," Schmaderer said. queue.title: Texas attorney general-elect refuses to defend Ten Commandments classroom law
queue.dek: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson says he won't defend the Ten Commandments law requiring displays in every public school classroom.
queue.opening: Texas Attorney General -elect Nathan Johnson said this week that he won't defend a law requiring public schools across the state to display the Ten Commandments as the U.S. Supreme Court weighs whether to review the case. In an interview with The Dallas Morning News , Johnson, the first Democrat to be elected Texas attorney general in nearly three decades, called the law "unconstitutional," marking a distinct split with outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who championed the bill. "My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional," Johnson said. "The court will have the ultimate say as to what's constitutional and what is not, but I'm the one who says what the state's position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken," he continued. TEXAS DEM JAMES TALARICO RIPS 'UN-CHRISTIAN' COURT DECISION ON WHAT'S ALLOWED IN CLASSROOMS Under state law, Senate Bill 10 requires that a "conspicuous" copy of the Ten Commandments be displayed in every classroom in every public school and open-enrollment charter school across Texas. In April, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the law did not violate the Constitution, a major victory for proponents of the legislation, including religious freedom advocates, who have long argued the biblical text is a crucial component of America's legal, moral and historical heritage. queue.title: From turkey shortages to helicopter deliveries: The extraordinary history of Thanksgiving during war
queue.dek: The U.S. military has delivered Thanksgiving dinner to troops from Civil War Union troops to Vietnam's War Zone D, a tradition born in wartime.
queue.opening: In November 1966, 12 American soldiers stationed at an isolated outpost in a Vietnamese war zone were about as far from a traditional Thanksgiving at home as they could get. Their only means of resupply was by air. But the U.S. military was determined to get them Thanksgiving dinner anyway. A mess sergeant at Bien Hoa prepared turkey and all the trimmings, packed the meal into insulated containers and sent it by helicopter into War Zone D, where three officers and nine enlisted men of a 5th Special Forces detachment sat down to Thanksgiving dinner, according to Defense Department records preserved by the National Archives. The delivery was one piece of a massive logistical effort the U.S. military has undertaken during wars spanning generations to get traditional Thanksgiving meals to troops serving in combat zones. From civilians sending tens of thousands of turkeys to Union troops during the Civil War to helicopters carrying hot meals to soldiers in Korea, the holiday has been observed through some of the nation's most consequential conflicts. Thanksgiving became a national tradition in the midst of war. President Abraham Lincoln issued his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation as the Civil War entered its third year, calling on Americans to observe the final Thursday of November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise." The forecasts point to a season of cautious spending. Visa Business and Economics Insights expects holiday sales to increase 4.5% from last year — but after accounting for higher prices, the actual increase in what shoppers buy is projected to be just 1.1%. That makes it all the more important for shoppers to know what they’re paying for and whether a sale is truly a deal. "It's still a good time to shop. It's just that you just have to be a little bit more careful," Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, told Fox News Digital when discussing holiday and Black Friday shopping. 7 HOLIDAY SHOPPING SCAMS TO WATCH FOR THIS SEASON Gauri revealed that shopping during Black Friday does not always produce the best deal — especially when it comes to essential technology like cell phones. He advised shoppers to set a budget and research prices before making a purchase, especially for big-ticket items. "Have a number in mind and do your research before you go about spending the money," he said, recommending price-tracking sites and extra promotions.
